list.listitem: Suspect schizophrenia in patients with delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms such as flattening of affect. C

Patients with new onset psychosis should be assessed for a medical- or substance-related cause of their symptoms and for comorbid conditions. They should be assessed for suicidality and potential for violent behavior. C
Antipsychotic medication in moderate doses is effective for the treatment of schizophrenia. A
Treatment should be initiated as soon as possible. Delaying treatment may worsen long-term prognosis. B
There is no evidence that one antipsychotic medication or group is more effective than another, although they do differ in potential side effects. A

Antipsychotic medications are effective in preventing relapse. They should be continued for a minimum of 1 to 2 years in a first episode; indefinite treatment should be considered for multiple episodes. A

Patients with schizophrenia are at increased risk of developing general medical conditions than the general population, including circulatory, endocrine, gastrointestinal, hematological, pulmonary, and urogenital disorders. Thus, general medical health should be monitored in patients with schizophrenia. B

background.definition: Schizophrenia is a psychiatric disorder characterized by chronic psychosis which is generally preceded by an insidious decline in cognition. It exists on a spectrum of severity but almost always impairs social and occupational functioning. Symptoms are classified as positive symptoms, such as hallucinations or delusions. Negative symptoms include: flattened affect or poverty of speech; and impairments in cognition, including attention, memory and executive functions.

list.listitem: 0.22 per 1000 persons per year
Male:female incidence approximates 1.4:1
Peak age of onset in males 15 to 25 years, and in females 25 to 35 years
7 per 1000 in the general population; 10 per 1000 in patients >65 years of age
13% in offspring of one schizophrenic parent, 40% in offspring of both affected parents
50% concordance in monozygotic twins
80% of schizophrenics have no affected parent
Total estimated cost in United States was $32.5 billion in 1990; by 1995 the cost had increased to an estimated $65 billion.

Direct costs are estimated between 1.5% and 3% of total national health care expenditures for industrialized countries (2.5% in the US). Medicaid-financed hospital admissions alone for schizophrenia are estimated to be 930,000 patient days per year at a cost of over $800 million.
Indirect costs in lost productivity are estimated to be at least four times the direct cost. Direct and indirect costs exceed those of all cancers combined.
Schizophrenic patients represent 15% to 45% of homeless persons in America.

Depression, suicide, substance use and medical comorbidity, social isolation, joblessness, criminal victimization, physical or sexual abuse, and involvement in the criminal justice system are far more common in persons with schizophrenia.
No underlying cause or causes has been conclusively identified.

Current theory posits cause to be multifactorial, a combination of genetic vulnerability, perinatal insults, and subsequent other stressors. Theoretical insults include obstetrical complications or in utero exposure to viral or other agents, followed later by difficult family environments, substance abuse, and developmental stress.
See table for risk factors.
Pathophysiology is not clearly understood. Initial hypothesis was excess in dopaminergic transmission.
Current working hypothesis is dysregulation of a number of neurotransmitters including dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), and glutamate.
Enlargement in lateral and third ventricles and volume loss/structural abnormalities in the prefrontal cortex, limbic system, and thalamus are reported.
No current United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) screening guidelines exist for schizophrenia or psychotic disorders. C
There is no proven intervention to prevent schizophrenia in healthy, asymptomatic patients. B
Suspect schizophrenia in patients with delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms such as flattening of affect. C
Assess patients with psychosis for a medical- or substance-related cause, medical or psychiatric comorbidity, and the potential for violent or suicidal behavior. C
The following tests are recommended for all patients as part of their initial assessment: CBC, complete metabolic panel, liver functions, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), and test for syphilis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Symptoms in the presence of hallucinogens, stimulants, narcotics, and alcohol use
Symptoms in the presence of withdrawal from alcohol, narcotics, stimulants, and hallucinogen use
Much shorter course, association with medical illness
Anticholinergics, anxiolytics, digoxin, phenytoin, steroids, narcotics, and cimetidine
Duration >1 month but <6 months; does not require decline in functioning
Prominent depressive or manic symptoms for a substantial proportion of the illness
Delusions only that are not bizarre (i.e., erotomania)
Persistent pattern of perceptual distortion and odd behavior in the absence of frank psychotic symptoms
Too little clinical information available to classify

list.listitem: DSM V criteria: Two or more of the following characteristic symptoms are each present for a significant portion of time during a 6-month or longer period: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, or negative symptoms (i.e., affective flattening, alogia, or avolition).

Only one symptom required if delusions are bizarre or hallucinations consist of a voice keeping up a running commentary on the person's behavior or thoughts, or two or more voices conversing with each other.
If the total duration is <1 month, diagnosis is brief reactive psychosis.
If the total duration is 1 to 6 months, diagnosis is schizophreniform disorder.
Suspect schizophrenia in patients with delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms such as flattening of affect.

Patients often have a long prodromal phase (2-5 years) during which their functioning and self-care insidiously decline. Prodromal symptoms may include poor sleep, anxiety, irritability, depressed mood, loss of interest in school or other activity, social withdrawal, poor concentration, and poor hygiene. Late in the prodromal phase the patient may develop suspiciousness, perceptual abnormalities, or other attenuated positive symptoms.
Prodromal phase symptoms can be difficult to distinguish from normal adolescence. Not all patients with prodromal symptoms go on to develop schizophrenia.

Positive symptoms of psychosis include hallucinations and delusional thoughts. Hallucinations are typically auditory, consisting of one or more voices that comment on the patient's thoughts or discuss the patient. Delusions are fixed, false beliefs that are not culturally appropriate. They may be persecutory, grandiose, religious, or extremely bizarre in content. Grossly disorganized speech, thinking, or activity may be present.
Negative symptoms of schizophrenia include flattening of affect, apathy, alogia, or extreme ambivalence.

Behavior may range from agitated, to quietly paranoid, to catatonic. Patients often attend to internal stimuli such as hallucinations or delusional thoughts to the exclusion of their environment. They can appear distracted and be difficult to engage in conversation. Hygiene may be very poor and dress inappropriate or bizarre.
A thorough physical exam should yield no evidence of neurologic or other illness and no evidence of drug use sufficient to explain the symptoms.
The following tests are recommended for all patients as part of their initial assessment: CBC, complete metabolic panel, liver functions, TSH, and test for syphilis.
If clinically indicated, test for HIV disease and hepatitis C; consider pregnancy test for women of childbearing years.
Test for drug toxicology, heavy metal screen, EEG, and MRI if clinically indicated.
When a patient presents with psychotic symptoms, recognition, accurate diagnosis, and rapid treatment are key. Diagnosis is an ongoing process as the illness unfolds and may be fluid over time.
Medical illness, substance abuse, and medication effect should be ruled out as causes of the symptoms.
Patients should be assessed for comorbid psychiatric substance use and medical illness and assessed for potential suicidality or violent behavior.
Providers should attempt to engage the patient and the family in developing a diagnosis and treatment plan. Whenever possible obtain informed consent for the use of medications.
See for diagnostic algorithm.

Antipsychotics in moderate doses are effective in the treatment of schizophrenia and preventing relapse. While second-generation antipsychotics are usually recommended as the first-line treatment for a first episode schizophrenia in most patients, they are not more effective than first-generation drugs. A
Clozapine is more effective for patients with refractory psychosis, but due to increased risk of agranulocytosis is reserved for those who do not respond well to other antipsychotics. A
Treatment should be initiated as soon as possible. B Patients who have been treated successfully for a first episode of schizophrenia should be continued on medication for 1 to 2 years. A
Cognitive behavioral therapy should be offered to schizophrenic patients, and family intervention and education programs should be provided to patients and their families. B
Supported employment should be provided to any patient who wishes to work. C
Antipsychotic therapy is the mainstay of treatment for schizophrenia and should be started immediately when psychosis is recognized.

Selection of antipsychotic medication should be guided by the clinical situation, including the history of previous response and side effects, patient preference when possible, and an understanding of the side effects of first-generation and second-generation antipsychotics (Table 2).
The largest study to date of the efficacy and tolerability of first- and second-generation antipsychotics showed a large average dropout rate from all treatments of 74% over 18 months.

There was no clear advantage of second-generation drugs over first-generation other than a lower incidence of extra-pyramidal side effects. This advantage disappeared if moderate doses of first-generation drugs were used (the equivalent of <13 mg of haloperidol). The cost of second-generation drugs is significantly higher; they may also carry a larger risk of triggering weight gain, glucose intolerance, and increased lipid levels.
A network meta-analysis of 127 randomized trials evaluating 32 different antipsychotic agents found none that were clearly more effective in preventing relapse in adults with schizophrenia.
A network meta-analysis of 14 studies with 3925 patients concluded that both aripiprazole and brexpiprazole were more effective than placebo and were similarly effective compared to each other.
A network meta-analysis of 78 trials with 11,505 patients found that among long-acting injectable antipsychotics, paliperidone, aripiprazole, and olanzapine were the most effective.

An experimental drug (SEP-363856) works differently than other antipsychotics and is an agonist of 5-HT1a and TAAR1 receptors. In a randomized trial with 245 patients, compared to placebo there was a significantly larger improvement in a symptom scale. Adverse effects were somnolence and GI problems, with one cardiac death out of 120 patients in the SEP-363856 group. No patients developed extrapyramidal symptoms and there was no effect on lipids or blood sugar.

10% to 30% of patients have minimal or no response to medication. Another 30% have only a partial response. Adjunctive treatment with mood stabilizers, antidepressants, benzodiazepines, or ECT may be helpful in some patients with clear mood symptoms. There is very limited evidence for these strategies.
Two or more antipsychotic drugs should not be used concurrently, other than during a cross taper from one to another.
See for treatment algorithm.
Music therapy, if of sufficient duration, improves the overall mental state and functioning of patients.
There is insufficient evidence for or against the use of acupuncture, antioxidants, horticultural therapy, and yoga for schizophrenia.
Supported employment is more effective than vocational rehabilitation strategies.
Supportive employment should be made available to all patients who wish to work.

Social skills training (usually as part of rehabilitation therapy), as a means of alleviating distress and difficulty among patients with schizophrenia, appears to improve social skills and decrease relapse rates, based on very low quality evidence.
Dance therapy, based on moderate quality data, has insufficient evidence for schizophrenia.
RCTs evaluating the efficacy of occupational therapy delivered by specialists versus nonspecialists for patients with schizophrenia are unavailable.

Cognitive behavioral psychotherapy improves mental state, hospitalization rates, and residual symptoms but does not reduce relapse rates; it was not consistently more effective than supportive therapy.

Group cognitive behavioral therapy targeting symptoms of psychosis (CBTp) appears to be more effective than standard care or other psychological interventions in terms of overall mental state and global functioning scores, but comparable in terms of quality of life, service use, and study dropout rate. It is unclear whether brief versus standard duration CBTp is more effective.
There is limited evidence regarding cognitive rehabilitation therapy.
There is no evidence that psychodynamic psychotherapy is effective.
Psychoeducation programs that include family members significantly reduce relapse and readmission rates.
Family interventions to reduce high expressed emotion family styles showed mixed results, but indicate they reduce relapse rates and improve medication compliance.
The evidence is inconclusive for parenting interventions, humor-based therapy, peer support, and life skills programs for patients with schizophrenia.
Shared decision-making, based on low to very low certainty evidence, helps patients with mental health conditions feel more involved in their care, without lengthening appointment time.

Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), when combined with drug therapy, may be effective as an adjunctive treatment for those patients who fail to respond to drug therapy alone. Additionally, a 2019 Cochrane review found ECT, compared to standard care, to be effective in the medium-term for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, based on moderate-quality evidence. However, it is unclear whether adding ECT to standard care is beneficial.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and magnetic seizure therapy (MST) have insufficient evidence for the treatment of schizophrenia.

Tobacco use is more common among persons with schizophrenia. A pragmatic randomized trial of 526 adults found that a smoking cessation intervention customized to the patient and delivered by mental health specialists increased the likelihood of smoking cessation at 12 months (aOR 1.6, 95% CI 0.9-2.8) and at 6 months (aOR 2.4, 95% CI 1.2-4.7).
There are no RCTs to establish the efficacy of dietary advice for patients with schizophrenia.
Nidotherapy, which is aimed at environmental modification rather than direct treatment of schizophrenia, has insufficient evidence of efficacy or harm.

Video games played statically (non-exergame) appear less effective than cognitive remediation for improving cognitive function in patients with schizophrenia, but appears to have similar efficacy in all other outcomes. Bodily-controlled video games may be better than standard care in improving cognitive functioning and aerobic fitness, based on very limited evidence.
It is unclear if Avatar therapy is effective in decreasing auditory hallucinations in people with schizophrenia.
Information and communication technology (ICT) as a tool for patient education and support for patients with schizophrenia has unclear benefits compared to standard care.
Relapse rates are higher in the short, medium, and long term for patients who discontinue medication.
If a decision is made to stop medication, the taper should be gradual with no more than a 10% reduction per month.
If there have been more than 2 episodes in 5 years or multiple episodes over time, indefinite medication treatment is recommended.
Patients should be assessed for suicidal ideation and safety, and referred for hospitalization if needed.
Patients with a new diagnosis of psychosis should be emergently referred to specialty mental health services for diagnostic evaluation, treatment planning, and institution of medication.
If there is a delay in availability of specialty services, drug treatment should be begun in the interim per guideline recommendations.
Day hospitals are a less costly and effective option for many patients.
Intolerable medication side effects should be managed by reducing the dose of antipsychotic or changing medications when possible. Side effects reduce medication compliance.
Akathisia and pseudoparkinsonian side effects can masquerade as psychotic symptoms, prompting the erroneous use of higher doses of medication.
Anticholinergic and dopaminergic medications can ameliorate the neurologic side effects of antipsychotics.
Cognitive behavioral therapy was somewhat successful in preventing weight gain, more so than pharmacologic interventions.
Patients requiring hospitalization should be managed in a specialty mental health unit.

Weight C, blood sugar B, and lipid levels C should be monitored for patients taking antipsychotic medication. A behavioral weight loss intervention successfully reduced weight over 18 months in obese adults with schizophrenia. B
The risk of relapse is 30% per year in compliant patients; rates are higher for patients who taper off medication. A
For patients at clinical high risk for psychosis, 9% at 6 months, 15% at 1 year, and 25% at 2 years transition to psychosis.B
Untreated, schizophrenia follows a course of gradual deterioration with a relapsing-remitting pattern.
Untreated, 60% to 70% of patients relapse in 1 year, and 90% in 2 years.

For patients at clinical high risk for psychosis, a meta-analysis found the following rates of transition to psychosis: 9% at 6 months, 15% at 1 year, and 25% at 2 years, and 27% at 4 years. Study level risk factors for transition include studies with more women and studies of patients with a higher proprtion of brief limited intermittent psychotic symptoms.
An episode of schizophrenia can be divided into prodromal, acute, stabilization/recovery, and stable phases. The recovery phase lasts 6 to 18 months after acute treatment.

During the stable phase persistent symptoms are relatively consistent in intensity. Subsequent prodromal periods last about 4 weeks, with behavioral changes and increasing emotional distress heralding the development of recurrent psychotic symptoms.

The period of 5 years after recovery from a first episode is known as the early course; further deterioration is most likely to occur during this period. More than 80% of patients achieved remission relapse in the first 5 years and, if not, continued on medication.

Most patients have a relapsing and remitting course with overall deterioration in functioning; 1 year relapse rates range from 0% to 46%. In compliant patients, the risk of relapse is 30% per year. Relapse rates are higher for patients who taper off medication.
10% to 15% of patients with a first episode have no further episodes, and 10% to 15% of patients remain chronically psychotic.
4% to 10% of schizophrenic patients ultimately commit suicide, with the highest percentage in the first 5 years of psychotic illness.
Patients with schizophrenia have 2 to 4 times the all-cause mortality of the general population.
A systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 studies found that patients with schizophrenia have 1.4 times higher mortality from cancer than the general population.

Factors indicating a better prognosis include female gender, family history of affective disorder and no family history of schizophrenia, a higher level of premorbid functioning, higher IQ, being married, acute onset with a clear precipitant, later age on onset and advancing age in general, and a predominance of paranoid and positive symptoms over negative or disorganized symptoms.
For all antipsychotic medication: height, weight, and BMI every 6 months
For second-generation drugs: lipids every 6 months if abnormal; every 2 years if stable
For second-generation drugs: fasting glucose or hemoglobin A1C 4 months after starting therapy; screen for polydipsia/polyuria at every visit
For first-generation drugs: screen for abnormal involuntary movements every 6 months
Remain optimistic about the efficacy of treatment.
Adherence to a medication regimen is the most important factor in preventing relapse and further deterioration.
Consistent treatment lowers the risk of tardive dyskinesia; intermittent treatment increases the risk.

A comprehensive treatment program should include medication, cognitive behavioral psychotherapy, family education, and assessment for special programs such as assertive community treatment and supported employment.
Prevalence in patients over age 65 is 1%, with 85% of these patients living in the community.

With the aging of the baby boom generation, the number of elderly patients with schizophrenia will increase substantially. The majority of these patients will be covered by Medicare, which does not reimburse mental health services or outpatient services well, and has limited coverage for medications that are often very costly.

A large cohort study found an increased risk of death in older patients taking antipsychotics, both first and second generation. However, the study population were nursing home patients with behavioral issues, and it is unclear whether the findings apply to older schizophrenic patients.
Due to the later average age of onset, women with schizophrenia are in the peak childbearing years and often have children or become pregnant.
Most schizophrenic mothers lose custody of their children, with most children placed in intermittent foster care.
These patients often have poor nutrition, comorbid substance use, and lower rates of adequate prenatal care, leading to poor pregnancy outcomes.

Studies of the safety of medications in pregnancy are retrospective and have generally not been controlled for the impact of psychosis itself. The use of medications should be based on an individualized risk/benefit analysis. Existing case series show no increase in malformations with the use of the second-generation antipsychotics; however, these are limited in number.
Schizophrenia is relatively rare in children with a prevalence of <1 in 10,000. Onset of schizophrenia before age 14 is associated with very poor prognosis.

It can be difficult to distinguish schizophrenia from Asperger's or pervasive developmental disorder; developmental disorders do not have psychotic symptoms. In schizophrenia there is generally a decline from previous normal development.
Second-generation antipsychotics increase the risk of weight gain and adverse lipid profiles in children and adolescents.

cell.label: Medical illness, medication effect, substance use present?
Diagnosis present in the setting of affective symptoms?
Odd beliefs/perceptual distortions, but no overt criteria A symptoms?
Psychotic symptoms meet criteria A for >1 month, but <6 months total of all symptoms?
Psychotic symptoms meet criteria A for >1 month and total time of illness >6 months?
Schizophreniform disorder. Treat (see acute phase treatment algorithm). Symptoms persist?
Consider psychosis secondary to medical cause or substance use.
Choose an oral antipsychotic other than clozapine; titrate to target dose (see ) and observe for 6-8 weeks.
Maintenance treatment for 1-2 years; consider indefinite treatment, particularly if patient had previous episodes.
Switch to a different oral antipsychotic other than Clozapine for 6-8 week trail at target dose.
Consider trial of Clozapine after failure of two agents (at least one second-generation agent).
• Assess history of prior response and current clinical situation. Choose safest agent with history of positive response (first or second generation). • Titrate to target dose and observe 6-8 weeks.
